opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what's really interesting about Dyna is how simple and almost understated the idea is, especially given when it was written, around 1990. Sutton's basic argument was that you shouldn't treat learning, planning, and acting as three separate problems. In Dyna, the agent interacts with the real world, gets real experience, and uses it two ways. It directly updates its value function or policy, which is ordinary reinforcement learning. And it also learns a model of the world: if I'm in this state and take this action, what happens next and what reward do I get. Then it uses that model to generate imagined experience and learns from that too, with the same learning algorithm.

So in Dyna, planning is just learning from simulated experience. There's no separate symbolic planner or search procedure bolted on. The world model is basically a source of extra data, a way to rehearse in your head. I find that framing beautiful, because it collapses the distinction between thinking and learning. When you plan, you're replaying and recombining what you know about the world to improve your behavior without paying the cost of real interaction.

What's striking to me, coming more from the vision and representation learning side, is that the argument for world models there is fundamentally about efficiency and generalization. Real-world interaction is expensive, slow, sometimes dangerous. If you have an internal model, even an imperfect one, you can squeeze much more out of every bit of real experience. That's exactly the argument many of us are making today for building world models for embodied agents and robotics. Thirty-some years later, the core logic hasn't changed.

But the world model in Dyna is very simple, tabular in the original experiments, small grid worlds, a lookup of state transitions. The hard part Dyna didn't have to face is the one we're stuck on now: what does a world model look like when the world is high-dimensional, visual, continuous, and partially observable? You can't just predict the next state as a table entry. Do you predict pixels? A latent representation? Which aspects of the world matter? So for me, Dyna gives you the "why," a very clean conceptual argument for why an intelligent agent should have an internal model and use it to imagine. The "how," especially how to learn good representations so the model is useful rather than just accurate at reconstructing pixels, is still wide open, and that's where I think a lot of the exciting work is today.

There's also something philosophically appealing in it. Sutton is often associated with the Bitter Lesson, the idea that general methods that scale with computation win. You might think that sits in tension with world models, which sound like building in structure. But Dyna shows it doesn't have to be. The model is learned from experience, not hand-designed, and planning is just more computation applied to learning. So in a way, world models done right fit the Bitter Lesson perfectly: you're turning compute into better behavior by letting the agent imagine.

r001.rationale: The response says Dyna combines direct reinforcement learning with a learned world model, and explains that imagined experience makes learning more efficient because real interaction is costly. This conveys reservations about relying on purely model-free learning.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as predicting what happens after an action in the current state, then says the agent uses that model to generate imagined experience for planning.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find fascinating about Dyna is how early Sutton was in framing the whole thing. This is 1990, 1991, and he's already saying: an agent shouldn't just learn from the real world, it should learn a model of the world and then learn from its own imagination. That's the core idea. Planning and learning are the same operation, just applied to different data, one real, one simulated by the model.

And the elegance is that he didn't try to make the model special. In Dyna the model is just something that takes a state and an action and gives you back the next state and a reward. Then you run exactly the same reinforcement learning update on those hallucinated transitions as you would on real experience. So the model is a data generator, a way to get more "experience" per unit of real interaction. I think that's the right way to think about it, and it's the thing people keep rediscovering. Dreamer, MuZero, a lot of the recent "learn in latent imagination" work is basically Dyna with a much better model.

The second thing that stays with me is his honesty about the hard part. The hard part is not the planning loop. It's the model itself. If the model is wrong, you plan beautifully toward the wrong world. Sutton knew that, and he sort of punted on it, because in 1990 you couldn't learn a good model of anything rich. And I'd argue that's still the open question today. For a tabular grid world, Dyna is trivial. For a camera stream, what does the model even represent? Pixels? Objects? Some latent space? That's where I spend most of my time thinking, because I come from vision, and I think the representation question is really the world model question.

So for me Sutton's argument is interesting less as an algorithm and more as a division of labor. He separated the problem into "how do you use a model" and "how do you get a model," and said the first one is basically solved if the second one is. I think he was right about that. What's changed is that now, with large self-supervised models, we might actually have a shot at the second one. And Sutton's other famous essay, the bitter lesson, kind of predicts how: don't hand-design the model, let it learn from scale. Those two ideas together are, I think, the real agenda.

r001.rationale: It says an agent should not learn only from real-world experience, but should also learn a model and learn from simulated experience, conveying reservations about purely model-free learning.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as mapping a state and action to the next state and reward, then using simulated transitions for planning and learning.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the connection between learning and planning. Usually we think of learning as something you do from real experience, and planning as something you do once you have a model. In Dyna, those two processes are brought together. You learn from interacting with the world, but you also learn from experience generated by your model, using essentially the same update mechanism.

That gives the world model a very concrete purpose: it lets you improve your behavior without having to take every action in the real world. The interesting question then becomes, what does the model need to capture to make that useful? Predicting everything accurately and predicting what matters for a decision aren’t necessarily the same objective. To me, that connection between the model and how an agent actually uses it is the compelling part.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining learning and planning in Dyna, but does not express reservations about purely model-free reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says model-generated experience can improve behavior without real-world actions, but does not state that predicting the next state from the current state enables planning.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that, in Dyna, the world model is useful because it lets the agent learn from experience it hasn’t directly had. You learn from interactions with the environment, but you also learn a model, and then use that model to generate simulated experience. Both can improve the same value function or policy.

So learning and planning become closely connected. Planning is another way to learn, using experience generated by the model. And that gives you a concrete way to think about what makes a world model useful: does it help the agent make better decisions? The model doesn’t necessarily need to reproduce every detail of the world. It needs to capture the consequences that matter for acting.

r001.rationale: The response describes Dyna’s model-based learning and planning, but does not express reservations about purely model-free reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says the model generates simulated experience for planning, but does not state that it predicts the next state from the current state.
